teaching.causalExplanation: Australia has three time zones. Start with standard time, which runs for about half the year, from April to October. Western Australia uses Western Standard Time. The Northern Territory and South Australia use Central Standard Time. Queensland, New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania use Eastern Standard Time. You'll see them written A W S T, A C S T and A E S T, with the S for standard. Each zone keeps one time on all its clocks, rounded from the Sun's time, like we saw with longitude. Western time is two hours behind Eastern time. Central time is only half an hour behind Eastern, so it's an hour and a half ahead of Western. Half-hour zones are unusual, and that's what makes Adelaide and Darwin tricky. And the rule from longitude still holds. Moving west, the clocks are behind, so you take time off. Moving east, you add. Back to the July final, seven thirty pm in Melbourne, on Eastern time. Perth is two hours behind, so fans there tune in at five thirty pm. Adelaide is half an hour behind, so seven pm. Darwin shares Central time with Adelaide, so it's seven pm there as well. Brisbane is in the same zone as Melbourne, so it's seven thirty there too. On a twenty-four-hour clock, that's seventeen thirty, nineteen hundred and nineteen thirty. Find the gap between the zones, decide ahead or behind, then add it or take it off. Now summer. Daylight saving means moving the clocks forward one hour for the warmer months, so there's an extra hour of daylight in the evening. In Australia it starts on the first Sunday in October and ends on the first Sunday in April. But not every state does it. New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia go forward. Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia don't. Watch the map as the months roll from July to January. The south-east jumps an hour ahead, and three zones split into five different times. When daylight saving ends in April, those clocks go back an hour, and the five times become three again. Sydney is now three hours ahead of Perth, an hour ahead of Brisbane, and an hour and a half ahead of Darwin. And here's the strangest part. In winter, Brisbane is half an hour ahead of Adelaide. In summer, Adelaide is half an hour ahead of Brisbane, even though it's further west.

scenes.teachingReason: Australia has three time zones. Start with standard time, which runs for about half the year, from April to October. Western Australia uses Western Standard Time. The Northern Territory and South Australia use Central Standard Time. Queensland, New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania use Eastern Standard Time. You'll see them written A W S T, A C S T and A E S T, with the S for standard. Each zone keeps one time on all its clocks, rounded from the Sun's time, like we saw with longitude. Western time is two hours behind Eastern time. Central time is only half an hour behind Eastern, so it's an hour and a half ahead of Western. Half-hour zones are unusual, and that's what makes Adelaide and Darwin tricky. And the rule from longitude still holds. Moving west, the clocks are behind, so you take time off. Moving east, you add.

scenes.teachingReason: Now summer. Daylight saving means moving the clocks forward one hour for the warmer months, so there's an extra hour of daylight in the evening. In Australia it starts on the first Sunday in October and ends on the first Sunday in April. But not every state does it. New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia go forward. Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia don't. Watch the map as the months roll from July to January. The south-east jumps an hour ahead, and three zones split into five different times. When daylight saving ends in April, those clocks go back an hour, and the five times become three again. Sydney is now three hours ahead of Perth, an hour ahead of Brisbane, and an hour and a half ahead of Darwin. And here's the strangest part. In winter, Brisbane is half an hour ahead of Adelaide. In summer, Adelaide is half an hour ahead of Brisbane, even though it's further west.

scenes.teachingReason: Time zones matter most when you travel. A plane leaves Perth at one pm in January, and the flight takes four and a half hours, an example time. Do the flight on Perth's clock first. One pm plus four and a half hours is five thirty pm, Perth time. Now convert. It's January, so Sydney is on daylight saving, three hours ahead of Perth. So the plane lands at eight thirty pm, Sydney time. Forget daylight saving, use two hours, and you'd say seven thirty, an hour early. The flight is still four and a half hours. Only the clocks have changed. Going the other way, the clocks work against you. A five hour flight leaving Sydney at nine am lands at two pm Sydney time, which is eleven am in Perth, just two hours after take-off by the clocks.

scenes.teachingReason: So that's Australia's clocks, three zones, with three times in winter and five in summer. But what about the rest of the world?
